extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV viewers, journalists, and researchers interested in Jimmy Kimmel Live! or late-night television production
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and procedural guidance about producing and formatting an American network late-night talk show, as illustrated by the Jimmy Kimmel Live! Wikipedia article. Covers schedule, format, set, recurring segments, personnel roles, censorship and regulatory issues, and special-broadcast practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show format and running time
rubrics_metrics.description: "Jimmy Kimmel Live! is an American late-night talk show... The nightly hour-long show tapes..." (infobox: Running time: 40 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure typically includes an opening/monologue, skits/bits, guest interviews, and a musical performance segment at the end (Jimmy Kimmel Live Concert Series). The article notes that runtime and format can change (e.g., during COVID-19 episodes were reduced to 30 minutes, later resumed to 60). Friday programming has shifted historically between new episodes, highlights ('This Week'), or rebroadcasts—producers should plan episode structure to fit both full and shortened runtimes and to allow for repackaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live versus taped broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Contrary to its name, the show has not regularly aired live since April 23, 2004..." and "it is recorded at 4:30 p.m. Pacific Time ... on the day of broadcast."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default production mode is taped same-day broadcast; 'live' editions are reserved for special events. The switch to taped broadcasts followed a censorship/bleep failure—producers should consider pre-recording to manage standards and practices risks, while reserving true live episodes for special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeslot and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally aired at 12:05 a.m. ET/PT; moved to 11:35 p.m. on January 8, 2013. Affiliate preemptions and syndication contracts have historically affected when the show actually airs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeslot affects audience size, lead-in competition (e.g., Tonight Show, Late Show), and episode structure (cold opens were dropped after the move). Producers must adapt format, timing, and repeats based on network scheduling and affiliate flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production location and set design
rubrics_metrics.description: The show tapes at El Capitan Entertainment Centre (Hollywood Masonic Temple) and has undergone multiple set changes; desk and chairs are not permanently staged and are often built out only after the monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set should support monologue center stage, allow quick transitions (e.g., building interview desk between segments), and incorporate modern video/display elements (like the "Wall of America") for flexible use in sketches and interviews. Design choices influence the kinds of bits and remote/telepresence interviews that can be presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold open and opening sequence conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: When at 12:05 ET the show began with a cold open; that device was dropped when moved to 11:35. Opening sequences have been revised many times (stop-motion, ILM-created sequence, shortened intros), and the announcer traditionally opens with a scripted phrase listing guests then says a closing line like 'And now... Here's Jimmy Kimmel!' (with variations over time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening format should match timeslot and episode pacing; announcer phrasing and intro length are part of branding and may be adapted for special episodes or tone shifts (e.g., omitting quips for Game Night specials). Temporary intro variations (e.g., 'Previously on...' segment) can be tried and discontinued based on reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: House band role and music
rubrics_metrics.description: The house band (The Cletones) plays the show's opening and closing themes and often plays through commercial breaks for the studio audience. The Jimmy Kimmel Live Concert Series comprises a musical performance at the end of the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dedicated band serves branding, pacing, and live-performance needs; producers should integrate band use into transitions and audience experience. Concert/artist segments are suitable as end-of-show features and can be sponsored; staffing and bandleader continuity affect show identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring segments and bits
rubrics_metrics.description: Show includes recurring features (e.g., 'Mean Tweets', 'Kids Table', 'Jimmy Kimmel Game Night') and long-running gags such as the 'We ran out of time' Matt Damon bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring segments help build the show's brand and viral potential but can also generate controversy (the 'Kids Table' segment drew protests). Producers should balance repeatable, audience-friendly bits with sensitivity to content that may offend groups or attract sustained backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest hosts and substitute programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest hosts filled in during hiatuses and special periods; a series of guest hosts did 30-minute episodes while Kimmel was on hiatus in 2020. The show historically used guest co-hosts and guest announcers in early seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a guest-host plan for planned and unplanned absences; use guest hosts to preserve continuity and experiment with formats. Guest-hosted episodes may be shorter or restructured; make clear audience expectations when host changes occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and practices, censorship, and regulatory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: A profanity barrage by Thomas Jane on April 23, 2004 led to moving away from live broadcasts; on August 15, 2019, ABC and the show were fined $395,000 by the FCC for misusing the Emergency Alert System (EAS) tone on an episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to broadcast standards and FCC regulations (avoid unauthorized use of EAS tones, ensure appropriate content timing/censoring). Failures can lead to fines, forced format changes (taping), and reputational damage—build compliance checks into production workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political content and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The show 'increasingly became political satire, especially in the opening monologues, during the mid-2010s' and has addressed personal policy-related issues (e.g., healthcare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political monologues can engage audiences and define a show's voice but carry heightened risk of controversy, affiliate pushback, and regulatory scrutiny. Producers should weigh editorial stance, anticipate backlash, and coordinate with network and legal teams when commentary targets contentious topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience health, safety, and contingency policies
rubrics_metrics.description: During the COVID-19 pandemic the show suspended production, produced at-home episodes, reduced episode length, resumed production without audience, and later required attendees to have full vaccinations when audiences returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have contingency plans for remote production, audience-free tapings, and health/safety requirements (vaccination proof, distancing). Health orders and local public-health guidance should drive decisions about studio audiences and format adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsorship integration and branded segments
rubrics_metrics.description: The show used 'integrated commercials' in cold opens and the Concert Series has been sponsored by brands (Coors Light, Pontiac, Bud Light, Sony, AT&T, Samsung, Cîroc, Mercedes-Benz over different periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate sponsorships into recurring segments to offset costs and build partnerships, but plan for sponsor turnover and corporate events that may affect continuity (e.g., Pontiac sponsorship ended after GM bankruptcy). Maintain transparency and creative control to protect show identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special broadcasts and event tie-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Special live editions are occasionally broadcast after major events like the Academy Awards. From 2003 until 2022, basketball-themed 'Jimmy Kimmel Game Night' episodes aired as lead-in programming to ABC's NBA Finals coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan special editions to capitalize on network events and audience spikes; coordinate timing and format with network sports/award schedules. Be prepared to discontinue or modify tie-ins if scheduling or industry conditions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and intro/announcer stylistic consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The announcer historically begins by saying 'From Hollywood, it's Jimmy Kimmel Live! Tonight...' and ends openings with unique quips and a drawn-out '-el' on 'Jimmy Kimmel' to give the show uniqueness; this phrasing has evolved over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent intro phrasing and small performative trademarks (announcer quips, theme music) contribute to brand recognition. Producers may refresh intros periodically (new sequences, updated music) but should preserve signature elements that audiences associate with the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling controversies and affiliate relations
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2025, FCC chair warnings and controversial monologue remarks led to affiliates (Nexstar, Sinclair) pulling the show and ABC suspending production indefinitely; boycotts, petitions, employee safety concerns, and protests followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish rapid-response PR, legal, and affiliate-communication plans for controversy. Understand that content decisions can lead to affiliate preemptions, network suspensions, advertiser withdrawal, and wide public reaction—manage risk through editorial review and crisis planning.
